questions.q: How much oxygen does one person breathe in a day, and how much oxygen did NASA's MOXIE make on Mars in total?
questions.do: Read the opening of Stage 6 · Build the colony, or find the MOXIE and Oxygen per person rows in How far to trust it.
questions.a: About 0.84 kg a day. MOXIE made 122 g in total over 16 runs (2021 to 2023), at best 12 g an hour. That is less than a sixth of what one person breathes in a single day, so a colony needs much bigger oxygen plants.

questions.q: With a Starship-class rocket and a crew of 4, how much fuel does your Mars ship need for the trip, and how many tanker flights bring it?
questions.do: In Stage 1 pick Starship-class and Crew of 4, press Next stage, then read the boxes at the top of Stage 2.
questions.a: About 252 t of methane and oxygen for the 3.6 km/s burn (155 t of ship and kit × 1.63), brought by 3 tanker flights of 100 t each.

questions.q: Why test the base on the Moon before Mars, and how much water did LCROSS find in the soil of Cabeus crater?
questions.do: Read the opening of Stage 3 · Prove it at the Moon and its maths box.
questions.a: The Moon is only about 3 days away, so spare parts and help can arrive quickly; Mars is months away and reachable only when the planets line up. LCROSS found about 5.6% water by mass, so each tonne of soil holds about 56 kg of water, enough to make about 50 kg of oxygen.

questions.q: When did India's Mangalyaan leave Earth, how long did it cruise, and when did it reach Mars?
questions.a: It launched on 5 November 2013, cruised for 298 days after leaving Earth's orbit, and entered orbit round Mars on 24 September 2014. India was the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first try.

questions.q: What happened to the Opportunity rover in 2018, and why does it matter for a Mars colony's power?
questions.do: Read the second paragraph of Stage 6 · Build the colony, and find the Dust storm thickness row in How far to trust it.
questions.a: A planet-wide dust storm darkened the sky (optical depth 10.8) so much that Opportunity's solar panels could not keep it alive; it never woke up and NASA ended the mission in February 2019. A colony that relies only on solar power can lose almost all of it for weeks, which is why a fission reactor, which works day and night, is useful.
